newsitem.title: USA: Probe of Tyson continues, indictment not ruled out.
newsitem.headline: Probe of Tyson continues, indictment not ruled out.

text.p: A government investigation of giant poultry processor Tyson Foods is still continuing and a criminal indictment against the company and its top officials cannnot be ruled out, said sources close to the investigation on Tuesday.

"The investigation into the gratuity-giving conduct of Tyson Foods, including the individuals that are responsible for that in the Tyson structure, is active and ongoing," said one of the sources, who did not want to be identified.

"And the people who are involved with that are (Tyson chairman) Don Tyson, (media, government and public affairs director) Archie Shaffer, and (Tyson lobbyist) Jack Williams," said another source. "You can certainly not rule out an indictment against Tyson Foods and the responsible individuals."

An indictment was returned earlier Tuesday against Tyson lobbyist Jack Williams for lying to the FBI and the Agriculture Department's Office of Inspector General in the preliminary investigation of former USDA Secretary Mike Espy.
Espy resigned in 1994 amidst a swirl of accusations that he took illegal gratuities from companies his agency was in charge of regulating.
The indictment was the fifth set of indictments to be returned in the government's two-year probe of Espy, being conducted by Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz.

The special investigation was started due to charges that Espy broke federal laws by accepting gifts and favors from Tyson Foods and other concerns with business pending before the Agriculture Department.
Tyson officials have repeatedly denied trying to improperly influence the Clinton administration.

Henry Schuelke, attorney for Williams, said his client denies all charges and intends to vigorously fight the indictment. Schuelke said Williams will not agree to any out-of-court settlement with the government.

"Mr Williams intends to assert a vigorous defense to the indictment," said Schuelke. "He looks forward to putting the Independent Counsel to its proof. Once the jury's heard the entire case, he fully expects to be vindicated."
